docs.title: git checkout <commit-hash>
docs.text:
We can use git checkout to view a previous commit.

When using git log to view commit hashes, we just need the first 7 digits.

➜  Novel git:(main) ✗ git checkout 529bf25
Note: switching to '529bf25'.

You are in 'detached HEAD' state. You can look around, make experimental
changes and commit them, and you can discard any commits you make in this
state without impacting any branches by switching back to a branch.

If you want to create a new branch to retain commits you create, you may
do so (now or later) by using -c with the switch command. Example:

  git switch -c <new-branch-name>

Or undo this operation with:

  git switch -

Turn off this advice by setting config variable advice.detachedHead to false

HEAD is now at 529bf25 add more talking on chapter 1

➜  Novel git:(529bf25) git status
HEAD detached at 529bf25
nothing to commit, working tree clean

docs.title: detached HEAD state
docs.text:
• HEAD usually refers to a branch NOT a specific commit
  • When we checkout a particular commit, HEAD points at that commit rather than at the branch pointer.
  • What we can do:
  • Stay in detached HEAD to examine the contents of the old commit
  • Leave and go back to wherever you were before
  • Create a new branch and switch to it.

docs.title: Referencing commits
docs.text:
• useful when to refer the last commit
git checkout HEAD~1 ## refers to the commit before HEAD 
git checkout HEAD~2
  • useful when to switch back to the last branch
git switch -

docs.title: git reset <commit-hash>
docs.text: Reset the repo back to a specific commit. The commits between are ==deleted==. But associated changes are remained.

docs.title: git reset --hard <commit-hash>
docs.text: Reset both the commits and the changes. ==Everything is deleted==

docs.title: git revert <commit-hash>
docs.text:
Given one or more existing commits, revert the changes that the related patches introduce, and record some new commits that record them ==Go back to one of the old commit and create a new commit of the old version==

If you want to reverse some commits that other people already have on their machine, you should use revert.

docs.title: Git
docs.text: Git is a free and open source ==distributed version control system== designed to handle everything from small to very large projects with speed and efficiency.

docs.title: Version control
docs.text:
Version control is software that tracks and manages changes to files over time.

Version control systems generally allow users to revisit earlier versions of the files, compare changes between versions, undo changes, and a whole lot more.

docs.title: History of Git
docs.text:
• Linus Torvalds
  • April 2005

docs.title: Git vs. Github
docs.text:
Git is the version control software that runs locally on the machine.

Github is a service that host git repositories in the cloud and makes it easier to collaborate with other people.

docs.title: git init
docs.text:
To create a new git repository.

  • Do once per project
  • Initialize the repo in the top-level folder

This command creates an empty Git repository - basically a .git directory with subdirectories for objects, refs/heads, refs/tags, and template files. An initial branch without any commits will be created (see the --initial-branch option below for its name).

$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /Users/morningstar/Git/Codes/Basics/Novel/.git/

docs.title: A common mistake
docs.text:
• Git tracks a directory and all nested subdirectories
  • Do not init a repo inside of a repo
  • Before running git init, use git status to verify that you are not currently inside a repo
  • To delete a repo, locate the associated $.git$ directory and delete it

docs.title: Git diff
docs.text:
We can use git diff command to view changes between commits, branches, files, working directory, and more!

We often use git diff alongside commands like git status and git log to get a better picture if a repository and how it has changed over time.

docs.title: Comparing changes between last commit, working directory, and staging area
git diff
docs.text:
Without additional options, git diff lists all the changes in our working directory that are NOT staged for the next commt.

staging area: a place where soldiers meet and where military equipment is gathered before it is moved to another place

docs.text:
Last commit New changes red orange yellow greenbluepurple red orange yellow greenblueindigoviolet 
$ git diff

diff --git a/rainbow.txt b/rainbow.txt
index 0b75516..5ac6fae 100644
--- a/rainbow.txt
+++ b/rainbow.txt
@@ -3,4 +3,5 @@ orange
 yellow
 green
 blue
-purple

+indigo
+violet
\ No newline at end of file

docs.title: Compared Files
docs.text:
diff --git a/rainbow.txt b/rainbow.txt

  • For each comparison, Git explains which files it is comparing. Usually this is two versions of the same file.

  • Git also declares one file as 'a' and the other as 'b'

docs.title: File Metadata
docs.text:
index 0b75516..5ac6fae 100644
  • The first two numbers are the hashes of the two files being compared.
  • The last number is an internal file mode identifier.

docs.title: Markers
docs.text:
--- a/rainbow.txt
+++ b/rainbow.txt
  • File a and file b are each assigned a symbol.
  • File a gets a minus sign(-)
  • File b gets a plus sign(+)

docs.title: Chunks
docs.text:
@@ -3,4 +3,5 @@ orange
 yellow
 green
 blue
-purple
\ No newline at end of file
+indigo
+violet
\ No newline at end of file
  • A diff only shows portions or "chunks" that were modified.
  • A chunk also includes some unchanged lines before and after a change to procide some content

Chunk Header

  • Each chunk starts with a chunk header, found between @@ and @@
  • Form file a, 4 lines are extracted starting from line 3
  • From file b, 5 lines are extracted starting from line 3

Changes

  • Every line that changeed between the two files marked with either + or - symbol.
  • lines that begin with - come from file a
  • lines that begin with + come from file b

git diff --staged: from last commit to staging area

docs.title: Git stash
docs.text:
When I aim to switch to another branch with some changes that is trivial to commit, two different things may happen:

  1. My changes come with me to the destination branch
  2. Error if git detects conflicts

Git provides an easy way of stashing uncommitted changes so that we can return to them later, without having to make unnecessary commits.

Use git stash when you want to record the current state of the working directory and the index, but want to go back to a clean working directory. The command saves your local modifications away and reverts the working directory to match the HEAD commit.

docs.title: git stash or git stash save
docs.text: Take all uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged) and stash them, reverting the changes in your working copy.

docs.title: git stash pop
docs.text:
Remove the most recently stashed changes in your stash and reapply them to your working copy.

➜  StashingDemo git:(goodbye) ✗ git stash
Saved working directory and index state WIP on goodbye: b44e428 fix link bug

➜  StashingDemo git:(goodbye) git switch main  
Switched to branch 'main'

➜  StashingDemo git:(main) git switch goodbye 
Switched to branch 'goodbye'

➜  StashingDemo git:(goodbye) git stash pop
On branch goodbye
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   app.css
        modified:   index.html

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
Dropped refs/stash@{0} (36e9ce997d76e24b1700f7126f77d70a637e0d34)

docs.title: GIthub Basics
docs.text:
Github is a ==hosting platform== for git repositories. You can put your own Git repos on Github and access them from anywhere and share them with people around the world.

Beyond hosting repos, Github also provides additional collaboration features that are not native to Git (but are super useful). Basically, Github helps people share and ==collaborate== on repos.

  • Collaboration
  • Open source projects
  • Exposure
  • Stay up to date

docs.title: Cloning
docs.text:
Two ways to get and creating Projects

  • init
  • clone

docs.title: git clone <url>
docs.text:
Git will retrive all the files associated with the repository and will copy them to your local machine.

In addition, Git initializes a new repository on your machine, giving you access to the full Git history of the cloned project.

➜  cloning git clone https://github.com/gabrielecirulli/2048.git
Cloning into '2048'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 1315, done.
remote: Total 1315 (delta 0), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 1315
Receiving objects: 100% (1315/1315), 615.46 KiB | 1.53 MiB/s, done.
Resolving deltas: 100% (773/773), done.

After the clone, a plain git fetch without arguments will update all the remote-tracking branches, and a git pull without arguments will in addition merge the remote master branch into the current master branch

docs.title: SSH(Secure Shell Protocol) connect
docs.text:
Using the SSH protocol, you can connect and authenticate to remote servers and services. With SSH keys, you can connect to GitHub without supplying your username and personal access token at each visit. You can also use an SSH key to sign commits.

The file contain SSH key: ~.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

  1. generate a new private SSH key -- (local on my machine)
  2. add it to the SSH agent -- (github setting)

docs.title: Connect with Github -- Existing Repo
docs.text:
1. Create a new repo on Github
  2. Connect your local repo (remote)
  3. Push up the changes

Exisiting local repo + New remote repo == > git remote --> git push

docs.text:
The -u option allows us to set the ==upstream== of the branch we're pushing

Once we've set the upstream for a branch, we can use the git push shorthand which will push our current branch to the upstream. (It push the branch you current locate)

docs.title: Fetch
docs.text: Fetching allows us to download changes from a remote repository, BUT those changes will not be automatically integrated (merge) into our working files.

docs.title: git fetch <remote>
docs.text:
• Fetches branches and history from a specific remote repository.

  • git fetch defaults to origin

  • git fetch <remote> <branch> fetch from a specific branch

docs.title: Pull
docs.text:
Pulling retrieve changes from a remote repository and updates our HEAD branch with whatever changes are retrieved from the remote.

==git pull = git fetch + git merge==

docs.title: git pull <remote> <branch>
docs.text:
• Just like git merge
  • It matters where we run this command from.
  • It can results in merge conflicts

docs.title: git pull
docs.text:
• remote will default to origin
  • Branch will default to whatever tracking connection is configured for your current branch.
git fetch git pull Gets changes from remote branches Gets changes from remote branches Updates the remote-tracking changes, i.e. origin/main Updates the current branch, merging them in, i.e. main No merge Merge and conflicts Safe to do at anytime Not recommeded if you have uncommitted changes

docs.title: Public vs. Private
docs.text:
• Public repos are accessible to everyone on the internet.
  • Anyone can see and clone the repo
  • Private repos are only accessible to the owner and people who have been granted access.

docs.title: Collaborators
docs.text:
Settings -- Access --Collaborators

  • git push
  • git pull

docs.title: README.md
docs.text:
A README file is used to communicate important information about a repository including:

  • What the project does
  • How to run the project
  • Who maintains the project

If you put a README.md in the root of your project, Github will recognize it and automatically display it on the repo's home page.

Markdown cheatsheet

docs.title: Github Gists
docs.text:
Github Gists are a simple way to share code snippets and useful fragments with others.

Gists are much easier to create, but offer far fewer features than a typical Github Repository.

Profile --> Your gists

docs.title: Github Pages
docs.text:
Github pages are public webpages that are hosted and published via Github. They allow you to create a website simply by pushing you code to Github.

Github Pages is a hosting service for ==static webpages==, so it does not support server-side code.

  • User site
  • username.github.io
  • Project site
  • username.github.io/repo-name
$ git switch -c gh-pages

$ git touch index.html
$ git touch app.css
$ git touch app.js

$ git add .
$ git commit -m "Add github pages"
$ git push origin gh-pages

## Now you can find it in JoshTWang.github.io/CSEmpire

docs.title: Centralized Workflow
docs.text:
Everyone works on the master branch.

  • Lots of time spent solving confilicts and merging code
  • No one can work on anything without disturbing the main codebase
  • The only way to collaborate on a feature together is to push incomplete code to master

docs.title: Feature Branches
docs.text:
All new development should be done on seperate branches.

Treat main branch as the official project history.

docs.title: Feature branch naming
docs.text: Often you will see branch names that include slashes like bug/fix-scroll, feature/login-form

docs.title: Merging in feature branches
docs.text:
1. Merge whenever you want
  2. Email to discuss
  3. Pull Requests

docs.title: Pull Requests
docs.text:
1. Do some work locally on a fetch branch
  2. Push up the feature branch to Github
  3. Open a ==Pull Request== using the feature branch just pushed up to Github
  4. Wait for the PR to be approved and merged. Start a discussion on the PR.

Pull request --> add comment --> create pull request --> merge pull request

docs.title: Merging pull requests with conflicts
docs.text:
# step 1: merge the main branch into my-new-feature branch
git fetch origin
git switch my-new-feature
git merge main
fix conflicts

#step 2: merge the resolved conflicts feature branch into main and push
git switch main
git merge --no--ff my-new-feature # no fast forward merge to create merging commit
git push origin main

docs.title: Branch protect rules
docs.text: Define branch protect rules to disable force push, prevent branches from deleted, and optionally require status check before merging.

docs.title: Fork & Clone
docs.text: Github allow us to create perdonal copies of other people's repositories. We call those copies a ==fork== of the original.

docs.title: Fork & Clone workflow
docs.text:
1. Fork the original project repo on Github
  2. Clone my fork to local machine
  3. git clone <my forked repo>
  4. Add a remote pointing to the original project repo. This remote is often named ==upstream== (pull new changes if any)
  5. git remote add upstream <other's repo>
  6. Make changes and add/commit on a feature branch on my local machine
  7. git commit -am
  8. Push up new feature branch to my forked repo ==origin==
  9. git push origin <new-feature>
  10. Open a pull request to the original project repo containing the new work
  11. Pull request is accepted or closed.

docs.title: git rebase <branch-name>
docs.text:
git-rebase - Reapply commits on top of another base tip

  • as an alternative to git merge
  • Current at $feat$, run git rebase main --> change the $feat$ branch --> add all commits in $feat$ at the top of all commits in $main$, main branch is untouched
  • as a cleanup tool
➜  RebaseDemo git:(feat) git rebase main
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feat.

Instead of using a merging commit, rebasing ==rewrites history== by creating new commits for each of the original feature branch commits and add those new commits at the end of master branch.

  • We get a much ==cleaner project history==. No unnecessary merge commits!
  • We end up with a ==linear== project history.

docs.title: Golden rules: when not to rebase
docs.text: Never rebase commits that have been shared with others (already pushed). You do not want to rewrite any git history that other people already have.

docs.title: Conflict in Rebasing
docs.text:
1. Resolve all conflicts manually
  2. git add <conflict files>
  3. git rebase --continue

OR

  1. git rebase absortto get the status before

docs.title: git rebase -i <commit-hash>
docs.text:
Interactive rebase will allows us to ==edit commits, add files, drop commit, etc==.

➜  interactive-rebase-demo git:(main) git switch -c feat


➜  interactive-rebase-demo git:(feat) git rebase -i HEAD~9
# Rebase 0e19c7a..3b23c17 onto 0e19c7a (9 commands)
#
# Commands:
# p, pick <commit> = use commit
# r, reword <commit> = use commit, but edit the commit message
# e, edit <commit> = use commit, but stop for amending
# s, squash <commit> = use commit, but meld into previous commit
# f, fixup [-C | -c] <commit> = like "squash" but keep only the previous
#                    commit's log message, unless -C is used, in which case
#                    keep only this commit's message; -c is same as -C but
#                    opens the editor
# x, exec <command> = run command (the rest of the line) using shell
# b, break = stop here (continue rebase later with 'git rebase --continue')
# d, drop <commit> = remove commit
# l, label <label> = label current HEAD with a name
# t, reset <label> = reset HEAD to a label
# m, merge [-C <commit> | -c <commit>] <label> [# <oneline>]
# .       create a merge commit using the original merge commit's
# .       message (or the oneline, if no original merge commit was
# .       specified); use -c <commit> to reword the commit message
#
# These lines can be re-ordered; they are executed from top to bottom.
#
# If you remove a line here THAT COMMIT WILL BE LOST.
#
# However, if you remove everything, the rebase will be aborted.

docs.title: Commonly used
docs.text:
• pick = use commit

  • reword = use commit, but edit the commit message

  • fixup [-C | -c] = meld current commit into previous commit (remove message but not changes)

  • drop = remove commit (remove message and changes)

    git commit --amend -- reword the previous command message

docs.title: Git Tags
docs.text:
Tags are pointers that refer to particular points in Git history.

Tags are most often used to mark ==version releases== in projects. (e.g. 2.4.1)

Two types:

  1. lightweight tags
  2. annotated tags

docs.title: Semantic Versioning
docs.text:
The semantic versioning spec outlines a standardized versioning system for software releases. $$ X.Y.Z $$ Z. Patch Release e.g. bug fixes

Y. Minor Release e.g. new feature

X. Major Release e.g. significant changes that is no longer backwards compatible

docs.title: git tag
docs.text: Print a list of all the tags in the current repository.

docs.title: git tag -l "<tag-name>"
docs.text:
• git tag -l "*beta*"
$ git tag
v16.9.0-alpha.0
v16.9.0-rc.0
v17.0.0
v17.0.1
v17.0.2
v18.0.0
v18.1.0
v18.2.0

docs.title: git checkout <tag-name>
docs.text: • detached HEAD

docs.title: git tag <tag-name>
docs.text: To create a lightweight tag. By default, Git will create the tag referring to the commit that HEAD is referencing.

docs.title: git tag -a <tag-name>
docs.text:
To create a new annotated tag. Git will open your default text editor and prompt you for additional information.

We can also use -m option to pass a message directly.

docs.title: git show <tag-name>
docs.text: To show the detial of the tag

docs.title: Pushing Tags
docs.text: By default, the git push command doesn't transfer tags to remote servers.

docs.title: git push --tag
docs.text: To push all tags at once.

docs.title: config File
docs.text:
The config file is for configuration. Unlick global configm it configure things on a per-repo basis.

[core]
    repositoryformatversion = 0
    filemode = true
    bare = false
    logallrefupdates = true
    ignorecase = true
    precomposeunicode = true
[remote "origin"]
    url = https://github.com/facebook/react.git
    fetch = +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*
[branch "main"]
    remote = origin
    merge = refs/heads/main

docs.title: refs Folder
docs.text:
• refs/heads contains one file per branch in a repository. Each file is named after a branch and contains the hash of the commit at the tip of the branch.
  • main, feat
  • refs/tags contains one file for for each tag
  • refs/remotes contains one folder for each remote, each remote has its own branch

docs.title: HEAD file
docs.text:
HEAD file is a text file that keeps track of where HEAD points.

refs/heaads/master
## OR ##
b2748907c3cffb226447417957f2608a7c60c27d

docs.title: Index file
docs.text: Index file is a binary file that contains a list of the files the repository is tracking. It stores the file names as well as some metadata for each file but not store the actual contents of files.

docs.title: Objects Folder
docs.text:
The objects directory contains all the repo files. This is where Git stores the backups of files, the commits in a repo, and more.

The files are all compressed and encrypted.

docs.title: 4 types of Git objects
docs.text:
• commit
  • tree
  • blob
  • annotated tag

docs.title: Hashing Functions
docs.text:
Git uses a hashing function called ==SHA-1==

SHA-1 always generates 40-digit hexadecimal numbers

The commit hashes are the output of SHA-1

docs.title: Git Database
docs.text:
Git is a key-value data store. We can insert any kind of content into a Git repository, and Git will hand us back a unique key we can later use to retrieve that content.

These keys are SHA-1 checksums.

docs.title: git hash-object <file>
docs.text:
The git hash-object command takes some data, stores in .git/objects directory and gives us back the unique SHA-1 hash.

➜  Object echo "hi" | git hash-object --stdin
45b983be36b73c0788dc9cbcb76cbb80fc7bb057
➜  Object echo "hi" | git hash-object --stdin
45b983be36b73c0788dc9cbcb76cbb80fc7bb057
  • Output are the same
  • echo simply repeats whatever we tell it to repeat.
  • --stdin tells git hash-object to use the content from stdin rather than file
$ echo "hi" | git hash-object --stdin -w
ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a
  • -w write the object to the database
  • We can find the change in ==.git/objects==

docs.title: git cat-file
docs.text:
Provide content or type and size information for repository objects

  • -p print
  • -t type
  • blob
  • tree
  • Commit
$ git cat-file -p ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a
hello

$ git hash-object dogs.txt -w

$ git cat-file -p 25030ba8 > dogs.txt

docs.title: Blobs
docs.text: Git blobs(binary large object) are the object type Git uses to store the contents of files in a given repository. Blobs don't even include the filenames of each file.

docs.title: Trees
docs.text:
Trees are Git objects used to store the contents of a directory. Each tree contains pointers that can refer to blobs and to other trees.

Each entry in a tree contains the SHA-1 hash of a blob or tree, as well as the mode, type, and filename.

List trees and blobs in the current pointer in main branch

➜  .git git:(main) git cat-file -p main^{tree}  
040000 tree 0a77c12ccb80520457fe55f3469dcdf85f7b6bb2    .circleci
040000 tree ee455b31da3561c3aec818359f774dcb01907388    .codesandbox
100644 blob 07552cfff88bafaf4d207e6255394bc6d6215302    .editorconfig
100644 blob 7d79ef692311259a6986aaa9160b1f6e7e795180    .eslintignore
100644 blob 0bc90137a5c7d2ad3e8a857943c24e43d7343dbd    .eslintrc.js
100644 blob 176a458f94e0ea5272ce67c36bf30b6be9caf623    .gitattributes

➜  .git git:(main) git cat-file -p b96dcb0480a0b0be0727976e5202a1e7b23edc3f
MIT License

Copyright (c) Facebook, Inc. and its affiliates.

docs.title: ==Commit==
docs.text:
Commit objects combine a tree object along with information about the context that led to the current tree.

Commit stores:

  • A tree object
  • A reference to parent commit
  • the author
  • the commiter
  • commit message

docs.title: ==What does git save==
docs.text:
Git does include for each commit a full copy of all the files, except that, for the content already present in the Git repo, the snapshot will simply point to said content rather than duplicate it. That also means that several files with the same content are stored only once.

So a ==snapshot== is basically a commit, referring to the content of a directory structure.

docs.title: Git reflog
docs.text:
Git keeps a record of when the tips of branches and other references were updated in the repo.

  • .git/logs/HEAD

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Git only keeps reflogs local
  • Git cleans out old entries after around 90 days.

docs.title: git reflog + show
docs.text:
The "show" subcommand (which is also the default, in the absence of any subcommands) shows the log of the reference provided in the command-line (or HEAD, by default). The reflog covers all recent actions, and in addition the HEAD reflog records branch switching. 

$ git reflog show HEAD

bd57b1e6e (HEAD -> donkey) HEAD@{0}: commit: add stupid file
b2748907c (origin/main, origin/HEAD, main) HEAD@{1}: checkout: moving from main to donkey

docs.title: Reflog references
docs.text:
name@{qualifier} ----- HEAD@{0}

We can use this syntax to access specific ref pointers and pay them to chekout, reset, or merge.

$ git checkout HEAD@{2} ## two moves ago

$ git checkout HEAD~2 ## two commits ago

docs.title: Timed references
docs.text:
We can filter reflogs entries by time/date by using temi qualifiers:

  • 1.day.ago
  • yesterday
  • 3.miniutes.ago
git diff main main@{yesterday}

git checkout bugfix@{one.week.ago}

docs.title: Rescue lost information with Reflog
docs.text: We can use reflog entries to access commits that seem lost and are not appearing in git log.

docs.title: Reflog with reset
docs.text:
When we run git reset --hard <commit-hash>, we will never find those commit in git log, but we can still get them in git reflog

➜  ReflogDemo git:(main) git reflog show main
5f44f46 (HEAD -> main) main@{0}: reset: moving to 5f44f46
5bee813 main@{1}: commit: add summer seeds
5f44f46 (HEAD -> main) main@{2}: commit: add more greens
4ace1e2 main@{3}: commit: plant winter veggies
36979ee main@{4}: commit (initial): initial commit

➜  ReflogDemo git:(main) git reset --hard main@{1}

Reset current HEAD to the specified state: that is the HEAD now will point to 5f44f46 which will go back to the state before reset.

docs.title: Reflog with rebase -i
docs.text:
Same idea

  1. git rebase -i HEAD~4 to edit previous commit
  2. OH NO! I do something wrong!
  3. git reflog show HEAD to find the state(commit-hash) we want to go back
  4. git reset --hard <commit-hash>

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
We can easily set up Git aliases to make our Git experience a bit simpler and faster.

[alias]
    s = status
    l = log
    a = add
    cm = commit -m
    ls = log --pretty=format:"%C(yellow)%h%Cred%d\\ %Creset%s%Cblue\\ [%cn]" --decorate
    ll = log --pretty=format:"%C(yellow)%h%Cred%d\\ %Creset%s%Cblue\\ [%cn]" --decorate --numstat
    la = "!git config -l | grep alias | cut -c 7-"

$ git config --global alias.s status

Some online aliases recommendation:

https://www.durdn.com/blog/2012/11/22/must-have-git-aliases-advanced-examples/

https://gist.github.com/mwhite/6887990

https://github.com/GitAlias/gitalias
